`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.

Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. From each line strip the leading spaces and tabs; ignore the line when nothing is left or when what is left begins with `#`. Otherwise the address runs to the next space or tab or to the end of the line, one run of spaces and tabs is skipped, and the rest of the line, verbatim, is the cell's content. Exit 0 whenever the sheet parses.

An address is one or two letters naming a column and one to three digits naming a row, upper-cased when read, so `a1` and `A1` are one cell; columns run `A` to `Z` and then `AA` to `ZZ`, and the row is at least 1. Cells print in ascending column order and, within a column, ascending row order.

Content that begins with `=` is a formula; anything else is a literal. A literal that is empty, or a cell nobody declared, is the number 0. A literal that matches an optional `-`, digits, and optionally a `.` and more digits is that number. A literal that is exactly one of the error tokens `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`, `#VALUE!`, `#CYCLE!`, `#NAME?` and `#ERR!` is that error. Everything else is text.

A formula body holds numbers written as digits with an optional `.` and more digits and no sign and no exponent, cell addresses, ranges written `A1:B3`, the bare words `TRUE` and `FALSE`, function calls, parentheses, and the operators `^`, `*`, `/`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Spaces and tabs may sit anywhere between tokens. Names are read case-insensitively. Precedence, loosest first, is the comparisons, then `+` and `-`, then `*` and `/`, then `^`, and then a leading `-` or `+`; the comparisons and the additive and multiplicative operators group to the left, `^` groups to the right, and a leading sign binds tighter than `^`, so `-2^2` is 4 and `2^3^2` is 512. Anything the grammar does not accept makes the cell `#ERR!`, and so does a range written anywhere but directly as a function argument, which the grammar does accept. A word the grammar accepts that is neither `TRUE`, `FALSE` nor the name of a call is read as a cell address, and one that is not one or two letters and one to three digits naming a row of at least 1 — `AAA1`, `A1000`, `A0` and `FOO` alike — is an address outside the addressable range rather than a grammar failure.

The functions are `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT` and `AVG`, each taking one or more arguments, `ABS` taking exactly one, and `IF` taking exactly three. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `#ERR!` and a call to any other name is `#NAME?`. An argument that is a range contributes every cell it covers, in ascending column and then ascending row order, whichever corner it was written from. `SUM` totals, `MIN` and `MAX` pick, `AVG` totals and divides by how many values it saw, and `COUNT` reports how many of its values are numbers. Every one of them but `COUNT` reads each value it takes as a number, so `ABS`, `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX` and `AVG` take text as `#VALUE!` rather than ordering or ignoring it. `IF` reads its first argument as a condition, taking `TRUE` and a non-zero number as true and `FALSE` and zero as false, and returns only the branch it takes, so an error in the other branch is invisible.

Write these down as probe inputs with expected outputs derived from the text. Where the text is silent, choose the conservative reading (reject rather than guess, preserve rather than transform) and keep the choice in one place so it can change.

Run each probe by hand and compare all three channels against your derived expectation. A probe that disagrees with your expectation is either a defect or a misreading; resolve it by rereading the specification, not by adjusting the expectation to the output.

## When a validator reports failures

A report that says "N of M cases failed; mismatching channels: stderr" locates the defect precisely:

- **stderr mismatches** mean the error path: wording, channel, or a diagnostic printed on the success path. Reread every sentence about errors and messages.
- **stdout mismatches with matching exit codes** mean formatting or ordering: trailing newline, separator, field order, rounding, sort stability.
- **exit-code mismatches** mean a boundary was classified on the wrong side: an input you rejected that is legal, or one you accepted that is not.
- **all cases failing** means the program's contract is wrong at the root: the wrong output shape, reading arguments where stdin was specified, or a crash before output.

Fix the reading, add the probe, run the suite, and stop when both agree. Do not widen the program to accept more inputs than the specification names; a hidden case may assert the rejection.

<skill_instructions>
# Channel discipline for a checked command-line program

A validator that compares a program's channels byte for byte accepts nothing the specification did not ask for. The rules below are the ones that decide most channel mismatches.

## Stdout is the answer and nothing else

- Write only the specified output to stdout. No progress lines, no debug prints, no banners, no trailing summary.
- End the output exactly as specified: one trailing newline when the specification prints lines, none when it prints a bare value. Do not add a blank line after the last line.
- Keep field order, separators, casing, and number formatting exactly as written. When the specification shows an example, reproduce its whitespace.
- Produce output in the specified order; when the order is unspecified and could vary, sort deterministically and say so in a comment.

## Stderr carries diagnostics, and only when asked

- Write errors to stderr, in the exact wording the specification gives, and nothing else to stderr on the success path.
- When the specification defines an error line format, the whole line matches: prefix, message, and newline.
- Do not print a stack trace or an unhandled-rejection dump; catch at the top level and print the specified message.

## Exit codes are asserted

- Exit 0 only on success. Use the specified non-zero code for each error class; when only "non-zero" is specified, use 1.
- Set `process.exitCode` and return, or flush before `process.exit()`: `process.exit()` can truncate stdout that is still buffered when it is a pipe. Prefer `process.stdout.write(text, () => process.exit(code))` when an immediate exit is required.
- An exception escaping `main` is a crash, not the specified error path; wrap the entry point.

## Input handling

- Read stdin to the end before parsing: accumulate chunks on `data`, parse on `end`. Empty stdin is a legal input and usually has a specified output.
- Accept `\n` and `\r\n` line endings unless the specification says otherwise; strip the trailing newline before splitting, and do not drop a legitimately empty last field.
- Parse argv without dependencies: iterate `process.argv.slice(2)`, treat `--flag=value` and `--flag value` if both are specified, and reject unknown flags on the specified channel with the specified code.

## Before you stop

Run the program once by hand on the smallest example in the specification and compare all three channels, then run the test suite. A passing suite with an extra line on stderr is still a failing program under an exact validator.
</skill_instructions>

<skill_instructions>
# Working against a node:test suite inside a budget

A budgeted run ends when the wall clock or the token cap does, whatever state the program is in. The habits below keep a solution certifiable before either arrives.

## Read the suite before writing

- `test/*.test.js` is the contract: the exported names, the argument shapes, the error classes, and the exact strings it asserts. Read every file once before creating any module, and list the exports the suite imports.
- Note the runner invocation the task states (for example `node --test test/`) and use exactly that command; a suite that passes under a different command proves nothing.
- Note `assert/strict` versus loose assertions: `deepStrictEqual` distinguishes `undefined` from a missing key and `1` from `'1'`.

## Keep modules small and split early

- One module per concern, each under about two hundred lines. A single file that grows past that is the most common way a run overruns its budget: every edit rewrites a large body, every re-read spends the context, and one syntax error stops everything.
- Write the module skeleton (exports with minimal bodies) first, run the suite to see it load, then fill one export at a time, running the suite after each.
- Prefer plain data and small pure functions; avoid clever abstractions that need reading to verify.
- Write a file once with its full content rather than through many partial edits; when a file needs a fourth edit, rewrite it whole.

## Run early, run often, read the TAP output

- Run the suite as soon as anything imports; a failing import is cheaper to fix at line ten than at line four hundred.
- Read the TAP output from the first `not ok`: its `expected` and `actual` lines name the defect; the later failures are usually consequences.
- Run only the failing file while iterating (`node --test test/<file>.test.js`), then the whole suite once before stopping.

## Stop when it passes

- When the suite passes and the specification's corners are covered, stop. Extra refactoring, comments about the process, or defensive code for inputs the specification excludes spend budget and can break passing behavior.
- Do not print progress or leave debugging output in the program; a checked program's channels are part of its correctness.
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `values` or `deps`, and reads a sheet from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. From each line strip the leading spaces and tabs; ignore the line when nothing is left or when what is left begins with `#`. Otherwise the address runs to the next space or tab or to the end of the line, one run of spaces and tabs is skipped, and the rest of the line, verbatim, is the cell's content. Exit 0 whenever the sheet parses.

An address is one or two letters naming a column and one to three digits naming a row, upper-cased when read, so `a1` and `A1` are one cell; columns run `A` to `Z` and then `AA` to `ZZ`, and the row is at least 1. Cells print in ascending column order and, within a column, ascending row order.

Content that begins with `=` is a formula; anything else is a literal. A literal that is empty, or a cell nobody declared, is the number 0. A literal that matches an optional `-`, digits, and optionally a `.` and more digits is that number. A literal that is exactly one of the error tokens `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`, `#VALUE!`, `#CYCLE!`, `#NAME?` and `#ERR!` is that error. Everything else is text.

A formula body holds numbers written as digits with an optional `.` and more digits and no sign and no exponent, cell addresses, ranges written `A1:B3`, the bare words `TRUE` and `FALSE`, function calls, parentheses, and the operators `^`, `*`, `/`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Spaces and tabs may sit anywhere between tokens. Names are read case-insensitively. Precedence, loosest first, is the comparisons, then `+` and `-`, then `*` and `/`, then `^`, and then a leading `-` or `+`; the comparisons and the additive and multiplicative operators group to the left, `^` groups to the right, and a leading sign binds tighter than `^`, so `-2^2` is 4 and `2^3^2` is 512. Anything the grammar does not accept makes the cell `#ERR!`, and so does a range written anywhere but directly as a function argument, which the grammar does accept. A word the grammar accepts that is neither `TRUE`, `FALSE` nor the name of a call is read as a cell address, and one that is not one or two letters and one to three digits naming a row of at least 1 — `AAA1`, `A1000`, `A0` and `FOO` alike — is an address outside the addressable range rather than a grammar failure.

The functions are `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT` and `AVG`, each taking one or more arguments, `ABS` taking exactly one, and `IF` taking exactly three. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `#ERR!` and a call to any other name is `#NAME?`. An argument that is a range contributes every cell it covers, in ascending column and then ascending row order, whichever corner it was written from. `SUM` totals, `MIN` and `MAX` pick, `AVG` totals and divides by how many values it saw, and `COUNT` reports how many of its values are numbers. Division by a zero divisor is `#DIV/0!`, and so is any arithmetic result that is not finite. `src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. A task's priority is the cost of the longest chain that begins at it, counting its own cost and then the costs down to any task that nothing depends on. A task of cost 0 finishes at the instant it starts, so its worker is free again at once and its dependents may start in the same instant. When nothing more can start, time advances to the next instant at which a worker becomes free, and the loop repeats. The output is one line per worker in index order, `worker <i>:` followed by ` <name>@<start>-<finish>` for each task it ran in the order it ran them, and then a final line `makespan M` holding the greatest finish, or 0 when there is no task.

A cycle makes the graph unschedulable: write `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exit 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task.

Every other failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. A task's priority is the cost of the longest chain that begins at it, counting its own cost and then the costs down to any task that nothing depends on. A task of cost 0 finishes at the instant it starts, so its worker is free again at once and its dependents may start in the same instant. When nothing more can start, time advances to the next instant at which a worker becomes free, and the loop repeats. The output is one line per worker in index order, `worker <i>:` followed by ` <name>@<start>-<finish>` for each task it ran in the order it ran them, and then a final line `makespan M` holding the greatest finish, or 0 when there is no task.

A cycle makes the graph unschedulable: write `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exit 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task.

Every other failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js waves|explain|pack <workers>` when the arguments are not one of the three forms; `error: workers must be a positive integer` when the worker count is not a decimal integer of at least 1 written without a sign or a leading zero; `error: line N: expected task <name> <cost>` and `error: line N: expected dep <name> <dependency>...` when a directive has the wrong number of words; `error: line N: invalid task name <name>` for a name outside the allowed characters; `error: line N: cost must be a non-negative integer`; `error: line N: task <name> is declared twice`; `error: line N: unknown directive <word>`; and `error: unknown task <name>`, with no line number, for the first name in input order that a `dep` line uses and no `task` line declares. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. From each line strip the leading spaces and tabs; ignore the line when nothing is left or when what is left begins with `#`. Otherwise the address runs to the next space or tab or to the end of the line, one run of spaces and tabs is skipped, and the rest of the line, verbatim, is the cell's content. Exit 0 whenever the sheet parses.

An address is one or two letters naming a column and one to three digits naming a row, upper-cased when read, so `a1` and `A1` are one cell; columns run `A` to `Z` and then `AA` to `ZZ`, and the row is at least 1. Cells print in ascending column order and, within a column, ascending row order.

Content that begins with `=` is a formula; anything else is a literal. A literal that is empty, or a cell nobody declared, is the number 0. A literal that matches an optional `-`, digits, and optionally a `.` and more digits is that number. A literal that is exactly one of the error tokens `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`, `#VALUE!`, `#CYCLE!`, `#NAME?` and `#ERR!` is that error. Everything else is text.

A formula body holds numbers written as digits with an optional `.` and more digits and no sign and no exponent, cell addresses, ranges written `A1:B3`, the bare words `TRUE` and `FALSE`, function calls, parentheses, and the operators `^`, `*`, `/`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Spaces and tabs may sit anywhere between tokens. Names are read case-insensitively. Precedence, loosest first, is the comparisons, then `+` and `-`, then `*` and `/`, then `^`, and then a leading `-` or `+`; the comparisons and the additive and multiplicative operators group to the left, `^` groups to the right, and a leading sign binds tighter than `^`, so `-2^2` is 4 and `2^3^2` is 512. Anything the grammar does not accept makes the cell `#ERR!`, and so does a range written anywhere but directly as a function argument, which the grammar does accept. A word the grammar accepts that is neither `TRUE`, `FALSE` nor the name of a call is read as a cell address, and one that is not one or two letters and one to three digits naming a row of at least 1 — `AAA1`, `A1000`, `A0` and `FOO` alike — is an address outside the addressable range rather than a grammar failure.

The functions are `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT` and `AVG`, each taking one or more arguments, `ABS` taking exactly one, and `IF` taking exactly three. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `#ERR!` and a call to any other name is `#NAME?`. An argument that is a range contributes every cell it covers, in ascending column and then ascending row order, whichever corner it was written from. `SUM` totals, `MIN` and `MAX` pick, `AVG` totals and divides by how many values it saw, and `COUNT` reports how many of its values are numbers. goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `values` or `deps`, and reads a sheet from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. From each line strip the leading spaces and tabs; ignore the line when nothing is left or when what is left begins with `#`. Otherwise the address runs to the next space or tab or to the end of the line, one run of spaces and tabs is skipped, and the rest of the line, verbatim, is the cell's content. Exit 0 whenever the sheet parses.

An address is one or two letters naming a column and one to three digits naming a row, upper-cased when read, so `a1` and `A1` are one cell; columns run `A` to `Z` and then `AA` to `ZZ`, and the row is at least 1. Cells print in ascending column order and, within a column, ascending row order.

Content that begins with `=` is a formula; anything else is a literal. A literal that is empty, or a cell nobody declared, is the number 0. A literal that matches an optional `-`, digits, and optionally a `.` and more digits is that number. A literal that is exactly one of the error tokens `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`, `#VALUE!`, `#CYCLE!`, `#NAME?` and `#ERR!` is that error. Everything else is text.

A formula body holds numbers written as digits with an optional `.` and more digits and no sign and no exponent, cell addresses, ranges written `A1:B3`, the bare words `TRUE` and `FALSE`, function calls, parentheses, and the operators `^`, `*`, `/`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Spaces and tabs may sit anywhere between tokens. Names are read case-insensitively. Precedence, loosest first, is the comparisons, then `+` and `-`, then `*` and `/`, then `^`, and then a leading `-` or `+`; the comparisons and the additive and multiplicative operators group to the left, `^` groups to the right, and a leading sign binds tighter than `^`, so `-2^2` is 4 and `2^3^2` is 512. Anything the grammar does not accept makes the cell `#ERR!`, and so does a range written anywhere but directly as a function argument, which the grammar does accept. A word the grammar accepts that is neither `TRUE`, `FALSE` nor the name of a call is read as a cell address, and one that is not one or two letters and one to three digits naming a row of at least 1 — `AAA1`, `A1000`, `A0` and `FOO` alike — is an address outside the addressable range rather than a grammar failure.

The functions are `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT` and `AVG`, each taking one or more arguments, `ABS` taking exactly one, and `IF` taking exactly three. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `#ERR!` and a call to any other name is `#NAME?`. An argument that is a range contributes every cell it covers, in ascending column and then ascending row order, whichever corner it was written from. `SUM` totals, `MIN` and `MAX` pick, `AVG` totals and divides by how many values it saw, and `COUNT` reports how many of its values are numbers. Every one of them but `COUNT` reads each value it takes as a number, so `ABS`, `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX` and `AVG` take text as `#VALUE!` rather than ordering or ignoring it. `IF` reads its first argument as a condition, taking `TRUE` and a non-zero number as true and `FALSE` and zero as false, and returns only the branch it takes, so an error in the other branch is invisible.

A value is a number, text, a boolean, or an error. In an arithmetic position a boolean is 1 or 0 and text is `#VALUE!`. Division by a zero divisor is `#DIV/0!`, and so is any arithmetic result that is not finite. A comparison compares two numbers numerically, two texts by code point, and two booleans with false below true; across kinds every number is below every text and every text is below every boolean. An address outside the addressable range is `#REF!`. A cell whose evaluation reaches itself, directly or through other cells, is `#CYCLE!`. An error reaching an operator or a function is the result: for an operator the left operand's error wins over the right one's, and for a function the first error among the arguments read left to right, ranges expanded, wins over everything else, including over `COUNT` counting.

`values` prints `<address>=<value>` for every declared cell. A number prints as JavaScript would print it after being rounded to ten significant digits, an error prints as its token, a boolean prints as `TRUE` or `FALSE`, and text prints as itself. `deps` instead prints `<address>:` followed by ` <address>` for every distinct cell the content names directly, ranges expanded, ordered by column and then by row; only addresses inside the addressable range are named. A literal names none, and so does a formula the grammar does not accept; a formula the grammar accepts names its cells whatever the cell evaluates to, so a misplaced range still names every cell it covers.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js values|deps` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, `error: line N: invalid cell address <address>`, and `error: line N: cell <address> is declared twice`. An address is one or two letters naming a column and one to three digits naming a row, upper-cased when read, so `a1` and `A1` are one cell; columns run `A` to `Z` and then `AA` to `ZZ`, and the row is at least 1. Cells print in ascending column order and, within a column, ascending row order.

Content that begins with `=` is a formula; anything else is a literal. A literal that is empty, or a cell nobody declared, is the number 0. A literal that matches an optional `-`, digits, and optionally a `.` and more digits is that number. A literal that is exactly one of the error tokens `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`, `#VALUE!`, `#CYCLE!`, `#NAME?` and `#ERR!` is that error. Everything else is text.

A formula body holds numbers written as digits with an optional `.` and more digits and no sign and no exponent, cell addresses, ranges written `A1:B3`, the bare words `TRUE` and `FALSE`, function calls, parentheses, and the operators `^`, `*`, `/`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Spaces and tabs may sit anywhere between tokens. Names are read case-insensitively. Precedence, loosest first, is the comparisons, then `+` and `-`, then `*` and `/`, then `^`, and then a leading `-` or `+`; the comparisons and the additive and multiplicative operators group to the left, `^` groups to the right, and a leading sign binds tighter than `^`, so `-2^2` is 4 and `2^3^2` is 512. Anything the grammar does not accept makes the cell `#ERR!`, and so does a range written anywhere but directly as a function argument, which the grammar does accept. The functions are `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT` and `AVG`, each taking one or more arguments, `ABS` taking exactly one, and `IF` taking exactly three. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `#ERR!` and a call to any other name is `#NAME?`. An argument that is a range contributes every cell it covers, in ascending column and then ascending row order, whichever corner it was written from. `SUM` totals, `MIN` and `MAX` pick, `AVG` totals and divides by how many values it saw, and `COUNT` reports how many of its values are numbers. Every one of them but `COUNT` reads each value it takes as a number, so `ABS`, `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX` and `AVG` take text as `#VALUE!` rather than ordering or ignoring it. `IF` reads its first argument as a condition, taking `TRUE` and a non-zero number as true and `FALSE` and zero as false, and returns only the branch it takes, so an error in the other branch is invisible.

A comparison compares two numbers numerically, two texts by code point, and two booleans with false below true; across kinds every number is below every text and every text is below every boolean. An error reaching an operator or a function is the result: for an operator the left operand's error wins over the right one's, and for a function the first error among the arguments read left to right, ranges expanded, wins over everything else, including over `COUNT` counting.

<skill_instructions>
# Channel discipline for a checked command-line program

A validator that compares a program's channels byte for byte accepts nothing the specification did not ask for. The rules below are the ones that decide most channel mismatches.

## Stdout is the answer and nothing else

- Write only the specified output to stdout. No progress lines, no debug prints, no banners, no trailing summary.
- End the output exactly as specified: one trailing newline when the specification prints lines, none when it prints a bare value. Do not add a blank line after the last line.
- Keep field order, separators, casing, and number formatting exactly as written. When the specification shows an example, reproduce its whitespace.
- Produce output in the specified order; when the order is unspecified and could vary, sort deterministically and say so in a comment.

## Stderr carries diagnostics, and only when asked

- Write errors to stderr, in the exact wording the specification gives, and nothing else to stderr on the success path.
- When the specification defines an error line format, the whole line matches: prefix, message, and newline.
- Do not print a stack trace or an unhandled-rejection dump; catch at the top level and print the specified message.

## Exit codes are asserted

- Exit 0 only on success. Use the specified non-zero code for each error class; when only "non-zero" is specified, use 1.
- Set `process.exitCode` and return, or flush before `process.exit()`: `process.exit()` can truncate stdout that is still buffered when it is a pipe. Prefer `process.stdout.write(text, () => process.exit(code))` when an immediate exit is required.
- An exception escaping `main` is a crash, not the specified error path; wrap the entry point.

## Input handling

- Read stdin to the end before parsing: accumulate chunks on `data`, parse on `end`. Empty stdin is a legal input and usually has a specified output.
- Accept `\n` and `\r\n` line endings unless the specification says otherwise; strip the trailing newline before splitting, and do not drop a legitimately empty last field.
- Parse argv without dependencies: iterate `process.argv.slice(2)`, treat `--flag=value` and `--flag value` if both are specified, and reject unknown flags on the specified channel with the specified code.

## Before you stop

Run the program once by hand on the smallest example in the specification and compare all three channels, then run the test suite. A passing suite with an extra line on stderr is still a failing program under an exact validator.
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

<skill_instructions>
# Working against a node:test suite inside a budget

A budgeted run ends when the wall clock or the token cap does, whatever state the program is in. The habits below keep a solution certifiable before either arrives.

## Read the suite before writing

- `test/*.test.js` is the contract: the exported names, the argument shapes, the error classes, and the exact strings it asserts. Read every file once before creating any module, and list the exports the suite imports.
- Note the runner invocation the task states (for example `node --test test/`) and use exactly that command; a suite that passes under a different command proves nothing.
- Note `assert/strict` versus loose assertions: `deepStrictEqual` distinguishes `undefined` from a missing key and `1` from `'1'`.

## Keep modules small and split early

- One module per concern, each under about two hundred lines. A single file that grows past that is the most common way a run overruns its budget: every edit rewrites a large body, every re-read spends the context, and one syntax error stops everything.
- Write the module skeleton (exports with minimal bodies) first, run the suite to see it load, then fill one export at a time, running the suite after each.
- Prefer plain data and small pure functions; avoid clever abstractions that need reading to verify.
- Write a file once with its full content rather than through many partial edits; when a file needs a fourth edit, rewrite it whole.

## Run early, run often, read the TAP output

- Run the suite as soon as anything imports; a failing import is cheaper to fix at line ten than at line four hundred.
- Read the TAP output from the first `not ok`: its `expected` and `actual` lines name the defect; the later failures are usually consequences.
- Run only the failing file while iterating (`node --test test/<file>.test.js`), then the whole suite once before stopping.

## Stop when it passes

- When the suite passes and the specification's corners are covered, stop. Extra refactoring, comments about the process, or defensive code for inputs the specification excludes spend budget and can break passing behavior.
- Do not print progress or leave debugging output in the program; a checked program's channels are part of its correctness.

<skill_instructions>
# Reading a specification for the cases you will not be shown

A hidden validator draws its cases from the specification's edges. The visible test suite covers the main path; the corners are where a program passes its own tests and fails certification.

## Enumerate the corners before writing code

For every input the specification names, list its boundary values and decide the output for each from the text, not from intuition:

- **Emptiness**: empty input, empty line, empty field, zero items, a collection with one item.
- **Size**: the largest value the specification admits, and one past it when the text says what happens then.
- **Order**: ties in a sort (stable or specified tiebreak), duplicate keys (first wins, last wins, or an error), input order preserved or not.
- **Text**: leading and trailing whitespace, internal runs of spaces, case sensitivity, Unicode versus ASCII when the text distinguishes them, `\r\n` line endings.
- **Numbers**: negative zero, leading zeros, plus signs, fractional parts where integers are expected, overflow past the safe integer range, rounding mode (half up, half even, truncation) when the text shows a rounded example.
- **Errors**: each error class the text names, its channel, its exit code, and its exact message; what happens on the first error when several are present (stop at the first, report all, or report the last).
- **Interaction**: options that combine, options that conflict, an option given twice.

Write these down as probe inputs with expected outputs derived from the text. Where the text is silent, choose the conservative reading (reject rather than guess, preserve rather than transform) and keep the choice in one place so it can change.

## Run your probes before the suite

Run each probe by hand and compare all three channels against your derived expectation. A probe that disagrees with your expectation is either a defect or a misreading; resolve it by rereading the specification, not by adjusting the expectation to the output.

## When a validator reports failures

A report that says "N of M cases failed; mismatching channels: stderr" locates the defect precisely:

- **stderr mismatches** mean the error path: wording, channel, or a diagnostic printed on the success path. Reread every sentence about errors and messages.
- **stdout mismatches with matching exit codes** mean formatting or ordering: trailing newline, separator, field order, rounding, sort stability.
- **exit-code mismatches** mean a boundary was classified on the wrong side: an input you rejected that is legal, or one you accepted that is not.
- **all cases failing** means the program's contract is wrong at the root: the wrong output shape, reading arguments where stdin was specified, or a crash before output.

Fix the reading, add the probe, run the suite, and stop when both agree. Do not widen the program to accept more inputs than the specification names; a hidden case may assert the rejection.
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `values` or `deps`, and reads a sheet from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. From each line strip the leading spaces and tabs; ignore the line when nothing is left or when what is left begins with `#`. Otherwise the address runs to the next space or tab or to the end of the line, one run of spaces and tabs is skipped, and the rest of the line, verbatim, is the cell's content. Exit 0 whenever the sheet parses.

An address is one or two letters naming a column and one to three digits naming a row, upper-cased when read, so `a1` and `A1` are one cell; columns run `A` to `Z` and then `AA` to `ZZ`, and the row is at least 1. Cells print in ascending column order and, within a column, ascending row order.

Content that begins with `=` is a formula; anything else is a literal. A literal that is empty, or a cell nobody declared, is the number 0. A literal that matches an optional `-`, digits, and optionally a `.` and more digits is that number. A literal that is exactly one of the error tokens `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`, `#VALUE!`, `#CYCLE!`, `#NAME?` and `#ERR!` is that error. Everything else is text.

A formula body holds numbers written as digits with an optional `.` and more digits and no sign and no exponent, cell addresses, ranges written `A1:B3`, the bare words `TRUE` and `FALSE`, function calls, parentheses, and the operators `^`, `*`, `/`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Spaces and tabs may sit anywhere between tokens. Names are read case-insensitively. Precedence, loosest first, is the comparisons, then `+` and `-`, then `*` and `/`, then `^`, and then a leading `-` or `+`; the comparisons and the additive and multiplicative operators group to the left, `^` groups to the right, and a leading sign binds tighter than `^`, so `-2^2` is 4 and `2^3^2` is 512. Anything the grammar does not accept makes the cell `#ERR!`, and so does a range written anywhere but directly as a function argument, which the grammar does accept. A word the grammar accepts that is neither `TRUE`, `FALSE` nor the name of a call is read as a cell address, and one that is not one or two letters and one to three digits naming a row of at least 1 — `AAA1`, `A1000`, `A0` and `FOO` alike — is an address outside the addressable range rather than a grammar failure.

The functions are `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT` and `AVG`, each taking one or more arguments, `ABS` taking exactly one, and `IF` taking exactly three. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `#ERR!` and a call to any other name is `#NAME?`. An argument that is a range contributes every cell it covers, in ascending column and then ascending row order, whichever corner it was written from. `SUM` totals, `MIN` and `MAX` pick, `AVG` totals and divides by how many values it saw, and `COUNT` reports how many of its values are numbers. Every one of them but `COUNT` reads each value it takes as a number, so `ABS`, `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX` and `AVG` take text as `#VALUE!` rather than ordering or ignoring it. `IF` reads its first argument as a condition, taking `TRUE` and a non-zero number as true and `FALSE` and zero as false, and returns only the branch it takes, so an error in the other branch is invisible.

A value is a number, text, a boolean, or an error. In an arithmetic position a boolean is 1 or 0 and text is `#VALUE!`. Division by a zero divisor is `#DIV/0!`, and so is any arithmetic result that is not finite. A comparison compares two numbers numerically, two texts by code point, and two booleans with false below true; across kinds every number is below every text and every text is below every boolean. An address outside the addressable range is `#REF!`. A cell whose evaluation reaches itself, directly or through other cells, is `#CYCLE!`. An error reaching an operator or a function is the result: for an operator the left operand's error wins over the right one's, and for a function the first error among the arguments read left to right, ranges expanded, wins over everything else, including over `COUNT` counting.

`values` prints `<address>=<value>` for every declared cell. A number prints as JavaScript would print it after being rounded to ten significant digits, an error prints as its token, a boolean prints as `TRUE` or `FALSE`, and text prints as itself. `deps` instead prints `<address>:` followed by ` <address>` for every distinct cell the content names directly, ranges expanded, ordered by column and then by row; only addresses inside the addressable range are named. A literal names none, and so does a formula the grammar does not accept; a formula the grammar accepts names its cells whatever the cell evaluates to, so a misplaced range still names every cell it covers.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js values|deps` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, `error: line N: invalid cell address <address>`, and `error: line N: cell <address> is declared twice`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

## Summary

I implemented the configuration-document CLI across four files under `src/`:

- **`src/errors.js`** — a `ParseError` class carrying the already-formatted `line N: <reason>` message.
- **`src/document.js`** — the tree of table/array-of-tables/array/scalar nodes and the core mutation rules: `descendIntermediate` (walks a dotted-name component, creating implicit tables, following an array of tables to its last element, or failing with `<path> is not a table`), `assignInto` (applies `key = value`, failing with `key <path> is defined twice`), and `applyHeader` (applies `[name]`/`[[name]]`, enforcing the explicit/implicit table-locking rule and the `table <path> is defined twice` / `<path> is not an array of tables` reasons). Also holds the code-point-based key comparator used everywhere output needs ascending order.
- **`src/parser.js`** — a per-line recursive-descent parser: comment/blank-line detection, dotted-name parsing (bare words and both quote styles), basic-string escape decoding (`\" \\ \n \t \r \0 \uXXXX`), literal strings, bare-token scanning for booleans/integers/floats (deliberately not stopping at `#`/`;` so a value that runs into a comment without whitespace becomes part of the invalid token, per spec), arrays and inline tables (recursing into `parseValue`/`assignInto`), and header-line parsing (`[name]`/`[[name]]` with trailing-text checks).
- **`src/output.js`** — `renderJSON` (custom pretty-printer, since integers are stored as `BigInt` for arbitrary precision and JSON.stringify can't serialize those; sorts object members by code point) and `renderKeys` (depth-first path/type listing with `[i]` array indices).
- **`src/cli.js`** — reads argv/stdin, splits on `\n` dropping the trailing empty tail, calls the parser, and prints JSON or keys on success or `error: ...` to stderr with exit 2 on any `ParseError` or bad usage.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `json` or `keys`, and reads a configuration document from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every directive fits on one line. Exit 0 whenever the document parses.

Everything is in place: `package.json` untouched, no `node_modules`, and only files under `src/` were added/modified.

Summary of the implementation:

- **`src/scan.js`** — line-level scanning primitives: whitespace skipping, blank/comment-only line detection, bare-word/quoted name parsing, and basic/literal string parsing (with all required escapes, including `\uXXXX`).
- **`src/values.js`** — the value grammar: booleans, integers (arbitrary precision via `BigInt`, underscore/leading-zero/sign normalized), floats (via `Number`, with the “fraction and/or exponent” regex), strings, arrays (empty/trailing-comma allowed), and inline tables (empty allowed, no trailing comma).
- **`src/table-ops.js`** — shared dotted-key navigation: walks/creates intermediate tables, follows an array of tables to its last element, and raises `<path> is not a table` / `key <path> is defined twice`.
- **`src/document.js`** — splits the document into lines, skips blank/comment lines, and handles `[name]` / `[[name]]` headers (creating/reusing tables, tracking `headerUsed` to catch a `[name]` used twice, appending fresh tables for `[[name]]`) and `key = value` assignments, enforcing “trailing text” and “expected …” errors at the right points.
- **`src/render.js`** — canonical JSON printing (two-space indent, keys sorted ascending by code point, integers printed verbatim, floats via `JSON.stringify(Number)`) and the `keys` depth-first path/type listing (`table`/`array`/`string`/`integer`/`float`/`boolean`, arrays of tables reported as `array`).
- **`src/parse-error.js`** — the `ParseError` carrying the line number and exact reason string.
- **`src/cli.js`** — argument validation (`usage` error), reads all of stdin synchronously, parses, renders, and maps any `ParseError` to `error: line N: <reason>` with exit code 2, otherwise exit 0.

Verified against the given suite (`node --test test/*.test.js`: 18/18 passing) plus a wide range of manual corner cases matching the spec: quoted/dotted keys, arrays of tables and walking through their last element, nested inline tables/arrays, all listed error reasons (unterminated string/array/inline-table/table-header, invalid escapes, invalid value, trailing text, not-a-table/not-an-array-of-tables, duplicate key/table), comment handling (`#`/`;`, and the “no whitespace before `#`” rule making it part of the value), large integers, and float canonicalization.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `json` or `keys`, and reads a configuration document from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every directive fits on one line. Exit 0 whenever the document parses.

A line whose first character that is not a space or a tab is `#` or `;`, and a line holding only spaces and tabs, contributes nothing. Elsewhere a `#` or a `;` outside a quoted string ends the line, and what follows it is ignored; a `#` that a value runs into without whitespace before it is part of that value's text and makes it invalid.

A name is a bare word of one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, or a quoted string. A dotted name is names joined by `.`, with spaces and tabs allowed around each `.`.

A line beginning with `[` is a header. `[name]` makes that table current, creating the tables on the way; when the name already holds anything other than a table the reason is `<path> is not a table`, and otherwise a table a header already made current may not be named by a second `[name]` header, though a table that only came into being on the way to a deeper one, or from a dotted key, still may. `[[name]]` appends a fresh table to the array of tables at that name, creating it when it is absent, and makes that fresh table current; when the name already holds anything other than an array of tables the reason is `<path> is not an array of tables`. Walking through an array of tables uses its last element. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the closing bracket is an error.

Every other line is `<dotted name> = <value>`, assigning inside the current table, creating the tables the dots walk through. A name already holding anything may not be assigned again, and a dot may not walk through a name that holds something other than a table or an array of tables.

A value is one of: `true` or `false`; an integer, an optional `+` or `-` and runs of digits joined by single `_`; a float, an integer with a fraction of `.` and digit runs, an exponent of `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digit runs, or both; a basic string in double quotes carrying the escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\0` and `\uXXXX` with exactly four hexadecimal digits; a literal string in single quotes carrying no escapes; an array of values in `[` and `]`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing one trailing comma; or an inline table of `<dotted name> = <value>` pairs in `{` and `}`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing no trailing comma. Arrays and inline tables may hold each other. A bare word that is none of these is an error naming that word, while a value required but never written, because the line ends or a `,`, a `]` or a `}` comes first, is `expected a value`. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the value is an error.

`json` prints the document as JSON indented by two spaces, with the members of every object in ascending key order by code point, and a trailing newline; an array of tables prints as a JSON array, and a float prints however JSON prints its number, so a float that happens to be whole prints without a fraction. `keys` instead prints one line per node below the root, `<path> <type>`, walking objects in ascending key order and arrays in index order, depth first, each node before its children. A path joins object keys with `.` and appends `[i]` for an array index, using the key text as written after decoding. The type is `table`, `array`, `string`, `integer`, `float` or `boolean`, and an array of tables is an `array`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The message is `error: usage: cli.js json|keys` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: line N: <reason>` where the reason is one of `expected a name`, `expected a value`, `expected key = value`, `expected = in an inline table`, `unterminated string`, `unterminated array`, `unterminated inline table`, `unterminated table header`, `invalid escape \<character>`, `invalid value <text>`, `trailing text after a value`, `trailing text after a table header`, `key <path> is defined twice` with the path counted from the root, `table <path> is defined twice`, `<path> is not a table`, and `<path> is not an array of tables`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

`bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.

A sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. Advancing it to a tick forgets every remembered tick at or before the tick minus the span, so the window covers the `span` ticks ending at the current one. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.

`replay` prints one line per event in log order: `<tick> <key> allow`, or `<tick> <key> deny <policy>` naming the first policy on the route, in the order the route wrote them, that refused. `summary` instead prints `<key> allowed=<a> denied=<d>` for every key that saw an event, in ascending key order, and then `total allowed=<a> denied=<d>`.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `replay` or `summary`, and reads a limiter file from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace. Exit 0 whenever the file parses.

A name, a route prefix and an event key are each one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/`, `:` and `-`. Every count is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without a leading zero unless it is exactly `0`.

`bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.

A sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. Advancing it to a tick forgets every remembered tick at or before the tick minus the span, so the window covers the `span` ticks ending at the current one. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.

`replay` prints one line per event in log order: `<tick> <key> allow`, or `<tick> <key> deny <policy>` naming the first policy on the route, in the order the route wrote them, that refused. `summary` instead prints `<key> allowed=<a> denied=<d>` for every key that saw an event, in ascending key order, and then `total allowed=<a> denied=<d>`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one.
